overview: The Umayyad emirate ruled much of al-Andalus from Córdoba between 756 and 929. Its mosques, neighbourhood workshops and household rubbish reveal a society being reshaped by Islamic rule. The imported map continues to 1000, crossing into the later caliphate, and its outline is only an approximation.

periods.title: The independent emirate
periods.summary: Abd al-Rahman I established an Umayyad state with Córdoba as its capital. Its authority and frontiers changed over time.

periods.title: The later caliphate
periods.summary: Abd al-Rahman III claimed the title of caliph in 929. This was a new political phase of the same dynasty.

items.text: The original Great Mosque arranged eleven aisles beneath two levels of arches. Reused Roman and Visigothic columns and other materials joined a new architectural design. Building skill included knowing how to give old stone a new job.

The earliest mosque floor was thick mortar laid over packed earth. Above it, decorated wooden beams supported the interior roof. Those details help us imagine the building before later generations added the features visitors see today.

sections.title: A neighbourhood of work and trade

items.text: Across the river, Saqunda developed a network of broad streets and smaller routes. Excavation plans reveal organised urban space with homes arranged around it. This early neighbourhood was not simply a tangle of houses that happened by accident.

Researchers identify a market, a lodging and trading building called a funduq, a metalworking workshop and an oil-production area at Saqunda. Large storage jars belonged to the same busy commercial landscape. Food, travellers and skilled labour all needed room.

Saqunda’s growth ended violently when its inhabitants rebelled against the emir in 818. The neighbourhood was destroyed and abandoned. Its short occupation helps archaeologists separate early emirate material from the much later splendour of caliphal Córdoba.

sections.title: Courtyard chores and the water run

items.text: In many excavated Saqunda houses, an open courtyard occupied roughly half the home. Hearths and household rubbish show that people prepared food and sometimes cooked there. The courtyard was working space, not just somewhere to admire a flowerpot.

Excavators found five wells within about 22,000 square metres of Saqunda. Three stood in open public spaces and probably served nearby residents. Carrying water was part of the neighbourhood’s routine; a private well in every house would be the wrong picture.

The excavated Saqunda homes did not have identifiable rooms set aside as latrines. Later caliphal houses were organised differently. This is a useful reminder that a famous city’s plumbing changed over centuries, and its earliest neighbourhoods cannot borrow later bathrooms.

A study of Saqunda rubbish pits counted 132 identifiable cooking-pot fragments and 167 jug or jar fragments among the diagnostic pottery. Broken everyday containers give archaeologists a kitchen inventory, even when the meals and the people who cooked them are long gone.

Three worked cattle shoulder bones from the rubbish pits were cut, smoothed and perforated. Researchers suggest that they may have served as writing surfaces for learning. No letters survive on these examples, so a school exercise is a plausible interpretation rather than a readable homework assignment.

A pottery fragment from Gitanos 8 preserves the Arabic words “الرحمن الرحيم”, meaning “the Compassionate, the Merciful”, within a religious formula. The published reading uses normal Arabic letter forms; the original cursive scratches lack dots. Archaeologists date the piece to the eighth or early ninth century.

The writer scratched the lettering after the pot had been fired. The hard surface made the point slip, leaving extra marks that complicate the second line. This small fragment brings writing out of royal documents and into the material world of a city neighbourhood.

ending.text: The emirate became a caliphate in 929 when Abd al-Rahman III claimed greater religious and political authority. Córdoba and its inhabitants continued into that new phase; 1000, the imported record’s endpoint, was not the emirate’s ending.
